C0.quote: compare voting behavior under simultaneous versus sequential voting
C0.note: Binary yes/no voting on a proposal under a threshold rule; equilibrium and experimental analysis of voting behaviour.

C1.quote: We report the results of an experimental voting game
C1.note: Section 2 derives equilibria (NE, SPE). Section 4 and the appendices report laboratory experiments, which make up most of the results.

C2.1.quote: players have two possible actions, called “Yes” and “No.”

C2.2.quote: players have two possible actions, called “Yes” and “No.”
C2.2.note: Binary Yes/No vote on a single proposal with a threshold k.

C2.3.quote: We define the true preference of N + as voting Yes
C2.3.note: Voters also have costs ci and benefits Gi as cardinal utilities.

C2.4.quote: The preferred outcome is not necessarily connected with the own confirmatory vote.
C2.4.note: True preferences (how a voter would vote if decisive) are defined separately from actual votes.

C3.1.quote: all players vote contrary to their true preferences
C3.1.note: Theory models votes as equilibrium strategies that may differ from true preferences. In the experiments, subjects choose their votes freely.

C4.1.note: Input format is OTH (binary votes), so the applicability condition is not met.

C4.2.note: The term 'dichotomous preferences' is not used.

C5.1.quote: The second is striving for efficiency (maximizing the sum of incomes)
C5.1.note: Outcomes are evaluated by the frequency of true majority results and by efficiency (sum of incomes).

C5.2.quote: the result is the same as if all voters had voted
C5.2.note: True majorities are defined on true preferences derived from costs and benefits, not on submitted votes.

VOT.quote_info: All players’ signs and cost/benefit ratios are common knowledge.
VOT.note: In the experiment, the strategy method left some uncertainty about predecessors' identities (footnote 11).

BRI.note: Outside pressure from party whips is represented only as voters' costs; whips do not act in the model.

C8.1.quote: sequential voting has a unique subgame perfect equilibrium
C8.1.note: Dominant strategies are applied to non-critical voters. Pure and mixed Nash equilibria are used for simultaneous voting. A bounded-rationality approach is used to explain deviations.

C1.reason: The strategic voting here is analysed only through equilibrium (EQ) and experiments (EM); there is no separate manipulation or strategyproofness analysis that would justify adding SB.

C6.VOT.reason: No analysis fixes voters' actions by the model, since experimental subjects choose freely and heuristics are only used to explain deviations, so STRAT fits better than MIXED.

C8.1.reason: The model explicitly uses dominant strategies to remove non-critical voters ('i has the dominant strategy to vote Yes'), so DOM belongs alongside NE, SPE and BND.
